16013-the-station-the-party-fight-and-fu:
William Carleton gathers three Irish sketches under one cover, all drawn from Catholic country life. The Station opens in a chapel where parish priest Philemy M'Guirk, after Mass, reads out the houses where the next week's Stations will be held, those home gatherings for prayer and confession. The Party Fight and Funeral and The Lough Derg Pilgrim complete the set with faction fighting and pilgrimage.

Dialect talk, local pride, and sharp comedy carry the sketches, but Carleton also shows faith as a lived, social force. Priests, neighbors, and pilgrims argue, feast, mourn, and pray in scenes full of Irish detail. Readers get three short, vivid windows on nineteenth-century Irish parish life in one volume.
17291-the-luck-of-thirteen-wanderings-an:
Mr. and Mrs. Jan Gordon tell their wanderings and flight through Montenegro and Serbia in this 1916 book, with photographs, a map, and color plates. Chapters run from Nish and Salonika to the Montenegrin front on the Drina, Cetinje, Scutari, Ipek, and Uskub. Then comes the flight of Serbia, Novi Bazar, the unknown road, and one more river to cross into Albania.

Jo at the machine gun fronts the volume, and diary pages add a firsthand voice to the retreat. The Gordons write with humor, grit, and a painter's eye for peasant dress and mountain roads. Readers of Great War flight and Balkan travel will find a vivid, human record of a small party in a great retreat.
21511-bell-s-cathedrals-the-priory-churc:
George Worley's guide to St Bartholomew-the-Great, Smithfield, came out in 1908 in Bell's Cathedral series. Worley also wrote on Southwark Cathedral and the Temple Church. His book gives a short history of the priory's founding and a full account of its fabric.

Forty-two pictures show the church, inside and out, including the view from the organ gallery. Worley points students to the great Monasticon account of the Smithfield foundation. He also treats the sister church of St Bartholomew-the-Less and the rule of the Austin canons. For walkers in old London, the book is a compact, learned companion.
24520-harbor-tales-down-north-with-an-ap:
Norman Duncan wrote these harbour tales of the Down North coast, the fishing shore of Newfoundland and Labrador, with an appreciation by Wilfred T. Grenfell. His stories follow harbour folk: fishermen, traders, maids, and rivals, in villages where the sea rules work and love alike.

One tale follows Elizabeth Luke, torn between two suitors, while another follows Pinch-a-Penny, a shopkeeper who raises the price of tea, pork, and flour in seasons of plenty. Duncan writes with warmth and dialect colour. Readers get a vivid picture of northern fishing life, its humour, hardship, and stubborn kindness.
24712-the-negro-at-work-in-new-york-city:
George Edmund Haynes wrote this study of the Negro at work in New York City, a study in economic progress. Haynes, a sociologist and a pioneer of Black social research, examines where Black New Yorkers worked, what they earned, and how they advanced, in the early twentieth century.

His chapters follow occupations, wages, unions, and migration, with tables and detail drawn from fieldwork. The study belongs to the first generation of scientific work on Black urban life. Readers of American social history will find it a landmark, careful, humane, and still instructive.
2649-captains-of-the-civil-war-a-chronic:
William Wood wrote this chronicle of the Civil War's captains for the Chronicles of America series, volume 31 in the Abraham Lincoln edition. Sixty years after Fort Sumter, Wood notes, the war still stood as the third and greatest modern civil war among English speaking peoples.

The book follows generals of the Blue and the Gray, never ignoring the politics that shaped their campaigns. Wood writes for general readers, with maps of character as well as battle. The chronicle serves as a clear, compact guide to the men who led armies, and to the war that remade America.
29024-across-mongolian-plains-a-naturali:
Roy Chapman Andrews wrote this 1921 book, Across Mongolian Plains: A Naturalist's Account of China's Great Northwest, published by D. Appleton in New York. Andrews, associate curator of mammals at the American Museum of Natural History and leader of its second Asiatic expedition, dedicates the book to Dr. J. A. Allen, whose knowledge and sympathy guided younger zoologists. His wife Yvette Borup Andrews took all the expedition's photographs.

A frontispiece shows a nomad of the Mongolian plains, and the text draws on Yvette's daily journals. Andrews writes of camps, trails, and the great northwest of China, with the eye of a museum man in the field. Readers get a classic of exploration writing, vivid and scientific at once, from the age before the great dinosaur hunts made Andrews famous.
33966-occurrence-of-the-garter-snake-tha:
Henry S. Fitch and T. Paul Maslin wrote this 1961 study of the garter snake in the Great Plains and Rocky Mountains, in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. The paper, pages 289 to 308 with four figures, traces the taxonomic history of Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis, first described as Coluber parietalis in 1823.

The type specimen came from Washington County, Nebraska, as the place is now known, on the Missouri River's west side near Boyer's River mouth. Fitch and Maslin map the snake's range across plains and mountains. The paper serves herpetologists who study western snakes.
9949-the-bark-covered-house-or-back-in-t:
William Nowlin, writing in the centennial year 1876, tells of real pioneer life in the Michigan wilderness. He left his farm in other men's care and spent the winter of 1875 writing, urged on by friends who had read his account, and the result is this firsthand memoir.

Chapters describe talking of Michigan, a first pig, and a second house with apple trees. There is a jug of whisky at a temperance meeting, lost cattle, hard times, a summer hunt, and visits from Indians. Nowlin writes plainly and with humor. Readers get the daily work, trouble, and fun of clearing a home in the woods.
captains-of-the-civil-war-a-chronicle-of:
William Wood wrote Captains of the Civil War for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale in 1921, sixty years after Fort Sumter. Wood, a Canadian colonel, announces a book of warriors that never ignores the politics behind them. Chapters run from the clash of 1861 through the naval and river wars to Gettysburg, Grant's hammering of 1864, Sherman's march, and the end in 1865.

Portraits anchor the campaigns: Lincoln as war statesman, Lee and Jackson in the east, Farragut on the water, Grant on the rivers and then the front. Maps and Brady photographs serve the text. Wood writes brisk, admiring military history for general readers, treating Blue and Gray captains in one chronicle, as his subtitle promises.
doe-osti-2589162-long-duration-energy-st:
Yonghong Chen of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory leads an eight-author, three-laboratory team in this report, NREL/TP-6A40-95548, dated September 2025. Ellie Estreich, Abdelrahman Ayad, and Bethany Frew write for NREL, Todd Levin, Audun Botterud, and Zhi Zhou for Argonne, and Tu Anh Nguyen for Sandia. Their subject is long-duration energy storage, systems that hold power for days, not hours, and the grid frameworks that fail to pay for them.

The team built its findings on stakeholder outreach, surveying the industry on what blocks deployment. Chapters cover the technology's values, the planning challenges of integrating it, and the modeling gaps that make it hard to value. Market design and policy mechanisms close the analysis. The core problem is incentive shape: multi-day reliability is worth a great deal to a grid, but most markets price energy by the hour, so the value goes uncounted and unbuilt.
doe-osti-3005299-gnss-installation-at-th:
Benjamin Männel, Markus Bradke, Florian Zus, and Marco Ramatschi, all at the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, report an installation in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-25-028, dated November 2025. They installed a GNSS receiver station at the Southern Great Plains observatory in Oklahoma. Navigation satellite signals bend through the atmosphere, and that bending reveals how much water vapor sits overhead.

Precipitable water vapor derived from GNSS is a proven climate monitoring quantity, as the team's earlier work shows. A permanent receiver at the observatory adds a continuous vapor record beside ARM's radiometers and soundings. Field campaign reports exist so later data users know exactly what was installed, where, and under what setup. The four-page report stays close to that purpose, closing with the references behind GNSS meteorology at the site.
doe-osti-3006464-adept-a-pedagogical-fra:
Pacific Northwest paper PNNL-SA-216605, dated October 2025, introduces ADEPT, the Agentic Discovery and Exploration Platform for Tools. Fourteen authors are listed, led by August George, Aivett Bilbao, and Khushbu Agarwal. The paper starts from a gap: language-model agents reason flexibly, while canonical scientific workflows are static and deterministic. ADEPT is a reference architecture and teaching framework meant to close that gap in the open, as a glass-box system.

Its design wraps established tools, naming BLAST and Nextflow pipelines as examples, and composes them into agent-driven workflows. The platform uses the Model Context Protocol for tool serving, LangGraph for agent orchestration, and an nsjail-based sandbox for safe code execution. The authors stress architectural clarity, safety, and modularity, and offer the system as an extensible blueprint for trustworthy AI-augmented research tools. Worked examples and probe transcripts fill the later pages.
doe-osti-3097330-cluster-dynamics-simula: Fission gas got cluster-simulated, and this DOE text models intra-granular bubbles. The pages detail the dynamics findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The evolution was pressure. The data were nuclear. The 2 were UO. The granular were intra.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergHaroldC: Harold Weisberg titled a monograph A Citizen's Dissent, and filled it with correspondence and notes on the Kennedy killing. The name states his position: one citizen refusing the official account. Weisberg's dissent rested on documents he gathered and letters he wrote over years. The monograph gathers that material in one place, showing how his case against the Warren Commission grew out of paper, not theory alone.
nasa-tm-19650021407-gemini-launch-vehicl:
Prepared in June 1963 by the Aerospace Corporation for NASA's Gemini program office, this report covers pilot safety for the Gemini launch vehicle at the Atlantic Missile Range. Report TOR-169 was made under an Air Force contract for the Space Systems Division. Gemini would carry two astronauts on a modified military rocket.

A safety program sets the rules that protect a crew on the pad and in early flight. It also protects people on the ground below the flight path. The report records how that program was organized at the range. Such planning rarely makes headlines, but every crewed launch rested on it.
nasa-tm-19720018347-aerodynamic-characte:
Ernald B Graves of the Langley Research Center reported these orbiter tests in May 1972, as NASA TM X-2561. The model was a space shuttle orbiter with a sixty degree swept delta wing. It formed part of the shuttle systems study program. Designers needed the shape's steady aerodynamic behavior before committing to it. Some control power tests were included in the program. The work ran in the Langley Unitary Plan wind tunnel.

Three supersonic speeds anchor the data set. They are Mach 2.50, Mach 3.90, and Mach 4.60. Flow density was held at a set Reynolds number per length. The results give the static forces and moments on the model. Control effectiveness readings show how well its surfaces could steer it. Such tables fed the shuttle's early design trade studies.
the-bark-covered-house-or-back-in-the-wo:
William Nowlin published his Michigan pioneer account in 1876, after spending much of the winter of 1875 writing it. Friends who read or heard the manuscript urged him to print it in the Centennial Year. Levi Bishop of Detroit, head of a county pioneer society, backed the book.

A key outlines the lives of John and Melinda Nowlin, their journey, and their settlement in Michigan. Scenes of forest life follow, with hopes, fears, and hard work, until clearing and farming bring what the key calls harvest home. Nowlin presents pioneer soldiers winning a long fight with nature to gain a home.
the-luck-of-thirteen-wanderings-and-flig: Mr. and Mrs. Jan Gordon wrote The Luck of Thirteen: Wanderings and Flight through Montenegro and Serbia, published in New York by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1916, with photographs, a map, and colour plates. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. Chapters shown include Nish and Salonika, Off to Montenegro, Across the Frontier, The Montenegrin Front on the Drina, Northern Montenegro, and To Cettinje. A frontispiece caption reads, Jo at the Machine Gun.
the-station-the-party-fight-and-funeral-:
This volume holds three tales by William Carleton. It is volume three, part two, of his collected works. The tales come from Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry. They are The Station, The Party Fight and Funeral, and The Lough Derg Pilgrim. The first opens in a chapel in Tir-neer, where the Reverend Philemy M'Guirk stands on the altar after Mass to announce the coming week's stations.

The priest calls on Jack Gallagher of Corraghnamoddagh, teasing him for seldom making part of the congregation and warning him to be prepared for Monday's station at his house. Carleton's comedy of parish life, Irish speech, and clerical banter runs through the announcement, setting the tone for the peasant tales that follow in the volume.
